questions.explanation: Copper plating runs Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e- at the anode and Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu at the cathode, which is the reverse of the spontaneous copper-zinc reaction, so the cell potential of the plating arrangement is -1.10 V and the reaction is nonspontaneous. A negative potential means the free energy rises, since delta G = -nFE is positive, so energy must be supplied. The spontaneously-fast option is simply false, and the missing-anode option is wrong because an electrolytic cell has both electrodes, with oxidation still at the anode.
questions.hint: Compare the direction of copper deposition with the direction of a copper-zinc cell.

questions.explanation: The reaction is nonspontaneous by 1.23 V, so a supply below 1.23 V cannot drive it and 1.23 V is the thermodynamic floor. The free energy confirms the size of the barrier: delta G = -nFE = -(4 mol e-)(96485 C/mol e-)(-1.23 J/C) = +475 kJ for the two moles of water written in the equation. Real cells need more on top of that, since overpotential and resistive loss add volts, which is why industrial water electrolysis runs at 1.8 V or higher. The tempting error treats the negative sign as if a supply had no magnitude, and doubling the figure is just as wrong, since the two electrode potentials are not additive in that way.
questions.hint: The supply has to overcome the magnitude of the negative cell potential.
questions.learningObjective: find the minimum applied voltage that can drive an electrolytic reaction

questions.explanation: Oxidation happens at the anode in every cell, and in molten sodium chloride the only species able to lose electrons is the chloride ion, which gives 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e- and produces chlorine gas at the positive electrode. The sodium ions migrate the other way and are reduced at the negative electrode, since they are attracted there and Na+ + e- -> Na is a strongly favorable step. The options that pair chloride with gain, or sodium with loss, are internally impossible, because neither ion can do the operation named.
questions.hint: In any electrolytic cell, oxidation still happens at the anode.

Being a metal is a category statement that says nothing about thermodynamics, which is the flaw. The option placing silver above hydrogen is the error the activity series is designed to prevent, and a power supply could force the dissolution but would not make it happen on its own.

questions.explanation: Oxidation gives Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-, and reduction needs Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu, so the two electrons on each side cancel and n = 2 mol of electrons per mole of reaction. This also shows why n matters in delta G = -nFE, where using 2 rather than 1 changes the free energy by a factor of two. The single-electron option is the most common slip, because zinc does lose two and students half-remember it. The zero option cannot be right, since no current would flow and no cell potential would be measurable.

questions.topic: Moles of electrons per mole of reaction

questions.explanation: Moles of electrons come first, 192970 C / 96485 C/mol = 2.000 mol, and since Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu needs two electrons per copper atom, that is 1.000 mol of Cu, and the mass is 1.000 mol x 63.55 g/mol = 63.55 g. A shorter route sees that one mole of copper needs exactly 2 x 96485 = 192970 C, so a charge of 192970 C deposits one mole of copper, 63.55 g, straight away. The tempting error forgets the two-to-one ratio and reports 127.10 g, twice what the circuit can actually plate.
questions.hint: Turn the charge into moles of electrons, halve them for Cu2+, then multiply by the molar mass.

questions.explanation: A galvanic battery holds a sealed, finite charge of reactants, so its voltage falls as they are consumed, while a fuel cell accepts hydrogen and oxygen from outside and expels water, so it can run as long as the feed lasts. Both are spontaneous galvanic devices, since the fuel cell reaction H2 plus half an O2 giving water has a positive potential of +1.23 V. Membrane versus salt bridge and platinum versus copper are design choices rather than the defining difference, since plenty of cells swap either one.

answer.exemplar: The nail is not one electrode but many tiny ones, because oxygen supply, moisture, and surface strain differ from spot to spot. Where iron is oxidized, Fe -> Fe2+ + 2e-, and those electrons travel through the iron itself to nearby spots where oxygen is reduced, so the nail short-circuits itself with no external wire. The iron therefore dissolves as Fe2+ and later forms the hydrated iron(III) oxide called rust, and the cell potential of about 0.40 to 0.80 V is enough to keep the process running as long as water and oxygen are present. Painting, galvanizing, and coating all work by cutting off one of those three requirements.

questions.explanation: Corrosion needs oxidation, reduction, and an electron path, and in a damp nail all three are present: Fe -> Fe2+ + 2e- at anodic spots, O2 + 2H2O + 4e- -> 4OH- at cathodic spots, and the iron itself carries the electrons between them. The potential driving it is the difference between the iron couple at about -0.44 V and the oxygen couple at about +0.40 V, so roughly 0.84 V is available and no external circuit is needed. The water is not incidental, since it carries the hydroxide and completes the circuit inside the film, which is why keeping steel dry stops rusting.
questions.hint: Look for places on the nail where oxidation and reduction can occur at the same time.
questions.learningObjective: explain rusting as a short-circuited galvanic cell
